rows.title: Northern gannet
rows.evidence: The northern gannet article says the specific name bassanus is from the Bass Rock in the Firth of Forth. The species is named for that island. The summary has no nest count.
rows.summary: The northern gannet (Morus bassanus) is a seabird, the largest species of the gannet family, Sulidae. The specific name bassanus is from the Bass Rock in the Firth of Forth.

rows.title: Manx shearwater
rows.evidence: The Manx shearwater article says three-quarters of the British and Irish birds breed on Skomer, Skokholm, and Rùm, so Skomer is one of the three principal strongholds. No nest count or coordinates are included.
rows.summary: The Manx shearwater (Puffinus puffinus) is a medium-sized shearwater in the seabird family Procellariidae. Three-quarters of the British and Irish birds breed on just three islands; Skomer, Skokholm, and Rùm.

rows.title: Glanville fritillary
rows.evidence: The article says the butterfly is highly restricted in the UK and confined to the Isle of Wight. No visit advice is included.
rows.summary: The Glanville fritillary (Melitaea cinxia) is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. The Glanville fritillary is a highly restricted species within the UK, being confined to the Isle of Wight and even there being largely limited to the southern coast.

rows.title: St Kilda house mouse
rows.evidence: The article says this extinct subspecies was found only on the St Kilda archipelago and calls it endemic. It is distinct from the St Kilda field mouse already listed.
rows.summary: The St Kilda house mouse (Mus musculus muralis) is an extinct subspecies of the house mouse found only on the islands of the St Kilda archipelago of northwest Scotland. When the last St Kildans were evacuated in 1930, the endemic house mouse became extinct very quickly, as it was associated strictly with human habitation.
